subject: Physics
name: Physics, Year 12
about: HSC, Mechanics, electromagnetism, light and the atom
syllabus: NSW Physics Stage 6 Syllabus (2017), Year 12 course, Modules 5 to 8

points.title: Projectile motion
points.brief: A projectile moves at constant horizontal velocity while gravity accelerates it downwards, so the two directions are treated separately.

points.title: Range and time of flight
points.brief: Launch speed and angle set how far and how long a projectile flies. Ignoring air resistance, 45° gives the longest range on level ground.

points.title: Uniform circular motion
points.brief: An object moving in a circle at constant speed is accelerating towards the centre. Centripetal force is F = mv²/r.

points.title: Banked curves
points.brief: Tilting a road lets part of the normal force supply the centripetal force, so cars can take the curve at a set speed without relying on friction.

points.title: Torque
points.brief: Torque is the turning effect of a force, τ = r F sin θ. A longer spanner gives more torque for the same force.

points.title: Newton's law of universal gravitation
points.brief: Every two masses attract with a force F = GMm/r², proportional to their masses and inversely to the square of their distance.

points.title: Gravitational field strength
points.brief: g = GM/r², the force per kilogram at a distance r from a mass. At the Earth's surface it is about 9.8 N/kg.

points.title: Orbital motion
points.brief: For a satellite, gravity provides the centripetal force. Its orbital speed depends only on the mass it orbits and the radius.

points.title: Kepler's laws
points.brief: Planets move in ellipses, sweep equal areas in equal times, and r³/T² is the same for every body orbiting the same central mass.

points.title: Escape velocity and gravitational potential energy
points.brief: Gravitational potential energy is U = -GMm/r. Escape velocity is the launch speed needed to leave a planet's gravity without further thrust.

points.title: Charges in electric fields
points.brief: A charge between parallel plates feels a constant force, F = qE with E = V/d, and moves like a projectile.

points.title: Charges in magnetic fields
points.brief: A moving charge in a magnetic field feels a force F = qvB sin θ at right angles to its motion, so it moves in a circle.

points.title: Force on a current-carrying wire
points.brief: A wire carrying current in a magnetic field feels a force F = BIL sin θ, whose direction follows the right-hand rule.

points.title: Force between parallel wires
points.brief: Two parallel wires attract if their currents run the same way and repel if opposite. The force per metre is μ₀I₁I₂/2πr.

points.title: DC motors
points.brief: Forces on the sides of a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field make it turn. A split-ring commutator reverses the current each half turn.

points.title: Magnetic flux
points.brief: Flux is the amount of magnetic field passing through an area, Φ = BA cos θ, measured in webers.

points.title: Faraday's law
points.brief: A changing magnetic flux induces an emf, and the faster the flux changes, the bigger the emf.

points.title: Lenz's law
points.brief: The induced current flows in the direction that opposes the change in flux that caused it, which follows from conservation of energy.

points.title: Generators
points.brief: Turning a coil in a magnetic field induces an alternating emf. Slip rings give AC and a commutator gives DC.

points.title: Back emf in motors
points.brief: A spinning motor coil acts as a generator, making an emf that opposes the supply. This is why motors draw most current when starting.

points.title: Transformers
points.brief: An alternating current in one coil induces an emf in another, with Vp/Vs = Np/Ns. Power lines use high voltage to cut energy lost as heat.

points.title: AC induction motors
points.brief: A rotating magnetic field induces currents in the rotor, which then turns to follow the field. They have no brushes and need little upkeep.

points.title: Maxwell and electromagnetic waves
points.brief: Maxwell predicted that changing electric and magnetic fields travel together as waves at the speed of light, so light is an electromagnetic wave.

points.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
points.brief: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma rays differ only in wavelength and frequency, and all travel at c in a vacuum.

points.title: Young's double slit experiment
points.brief: Light through two slits makes bright and dark bands, showing interference, which only waves do. Fringe spacing follows d sin θ = mλ.

points.title: Diffraction gratings
points.brief: Many narrow slits spread light into sharp bright lines, used to measure wavelengths and analyse spectra.

points.title: Polarisation
points.brief: Light waves can be filtered so they vibrate in one plane. Malus's law, I = I₀cos²θ, gives the intensity through a second filter.

points.title: Black body radiation
points.brief: Hot objects give off a spectrum whose peak wavelength gets shorter as they get hotter, as in Wien's law. Planck explained it with energy in packets.

points.title: Photons
points.brief: Light comes in packets of energy E = hf, so higher frequency light carries more energy per photon.

points.title: The photoelectric effect
points.brief: Light above a threshold frequency ejects electrons from a metal, however dim it is. Einstein explained this with photons, which the wave model could not.

points.title: Spectra and stars
points.brief: Emission and absorption lines identify the elements in a star, and a star's colour shows its surface temperature.

points.title: The postulates of special relativity
points.brief: The laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame, and the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for every observer.

points.title: Time dilation
points.brief: A moving clock runs slow compared with a stationary observer's, by the Lorentz factor. Muons from the upper atmosphere reaching the ground support this.

points.title: Length contraction
points.brief: A moving object is shorter along its direction of motion, as measured by a stationary observer.

points.title: Mass and energy
points.brief: E = mc² means mass is a form of energy. Relativistic momentum grows without limit as speed nears c, so nothing with mass reaches it.

units.title: From the universe to the atom

points.title: The Big Bang and expansion
points.brief: The universe began hot and dense and has been expanding since. Evidence includes the cosmic microwave background and red-shifted galaxies.

points.title: Hubble's law
points.brief: More distant galaxies move away faster, v = H₀d, which shows the universe is expanding.

points.title: The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram
points.brief: A plot of stars' luminosity against surface temperature, showing the main sequence, giants and white dwarfs, and how stars change over their lives.

points.title: Fusion in stars
points.brief: Stars release energy by fusing hydrogen into helium, through the proton-proton chain in smaller stars and the CNO cycle in larger ones.

points.title: Thomson and the electron
points.brief: Thomson's cathode ray experiments showed rays were made of negative particles, electrons, and measured their charge to mass ratio.

points.title: Millikan's oil drop experiment
points.brief: Millikan balanced charged oil drops in an electric field and found charge comes in whole multiples of the electron's charge.

points.title: Rutherford's nuclear model
points.brief: Alpha particles fired at gold foil mostly passed through, but a few bounced back, showing a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.

points.title: The Bohr model
points.brief: Electrons sit in fixed energy levels. Moving between them absorbs or emits a photon of set energy, explaining hydrogen's line spectrum.

points.title: Matter waves
points.brief: De Broglie proposed that particles have wavelengths, λ = h/mv. Electron diffraction confirmed it, and Schrödinger built a wave model of the atom.

points.title: Radioactive decay
points.brief: Unstable nuclei emit alpha particles, beta particles or gamma rays. Each has different charge, mass and penetrating power.

points.title: Half-life
points.brief: The time for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. It is constant for each isotope.

points.title: Mass defect and binding energy
points.brief: A nucleus has less mass than its separate parts. The missing mass is the binding energy, found with E = mc².

points.title: Fission and fusion
points.brief: Fission splits heavy nuclei and fusion joins light ones. Both release energy because the products are more tightly bound.

points.title: The standard model
points.brief: Matter is made of quarks and leptons, and forces are carried by particles such as photons and gluons. Protons and neutrons are made of quarks.
